overview.body:
**Anšar** (*anshar*) is the primordial sky of Babylonian cosmogony, the 'Whole Heaven' that arises from the mingling of the primordial waters Apsû and Tiāmat. With his consort Kišar, the Whole Earth, he forms the second generation of gods, the parents of Anu, and the ancestors of the great divine assembly.[^1]

The name is written 𒀭𒀭𒊹 in cuneiform. The Unicode restoration **Anšar** recovers the standard Assyriological transliteration, preserving the distinctive š consonant that ASCII loses; the entry is therefore Tier 1.[^2]

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.
Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.

the-name.body:
The name is attested in cuneiform as **𒀭𒀭𒊹** — the divine determinative followed by signs read An-šar. Its etymology is Akkadian: *an* 'heaven' + *šar* 'totality, whole', giving 'Whole Sky' or 'Totality of Heaven'.[^1]

The ASCII form *anshar* flattens the distinctive Akkadian consonant š to the digraph sh. The restoration **Anšar** recovers the standard scholarly form.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **a** → **A** — Same, capitalised
- **n** → **n** — Same
- **s** → **š** — S-caron: voiceless postalveolar fricative /ʃ/
- **h** → **—** — Dropped: digraph simplified
- **a** → **a** — Same
- **r** → **r** — Same

Because the restoration preserves the distinctive š, the name is Tier 1.

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.
The Assyrian Dictionary of the Oriental Institute of the University of Chicago (CAD).

pronunciation.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/anˈʃaːr/** — Akkadian Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **An-** — Open vowel [a] followed by alveolar nasal [n].
- **-šar** — Voiceless postalveolar fricative [ʃ], long [aː], and tapped [r].

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: 'ahn-SHAR' — the š is like the sh in 'ship', and the second syllable is drawn out.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Akkadian** — Anšar, 'Whole Sky'
- **Pair** — Kišar, 'Whole Earth'
- **Descendant** — Anu, the sky god born of Anšar and Kišar

Anšar is Tier 1 because the restoration preserves the postalveolar fricative š — a distinctive feature the ASCII form *anshar* loses.

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.

original-script.body:
The name is preserved in Sumero-Akkadian cuneiform as **𒀭𒀭𒊹** — cuneiform attested in copies of Enūma Eliš from the Old Babylonian period onward, in Mesopotamia.[^1]

The scholarly transliteration is *Anšar*, giving the normalised reading /anˈʃaːr/.

The rendering proceeds step by step:

- The name is written 𒀭𒀭𒊹 in cuneiform.
- The divine determinative 𒀭 marks the name as theonymic.
- The signs 𒀭𒊹 are read An-šar.
- The Unicode restoration Anšar is registrable in .com; the cuneiform form is not supported in the .com IDN table.

The appropriate label is 'Original Script and Scholarly Transliteration': the cuneiform is the attested writing, and Anšar is the standard scholarly reading.

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.
Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.
Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths.

domains.body:
Anšar is the **primordial sky** of Babylonian cosmogony. His domains cluster around the upper cosmos and cosmic order.[^1]

### Primordial Sky

The upper half of the cosmos, born from the mingling of fresh and salt waters.

### Father of Anu

With Kišar he begets Anu, the sky god, beginning the dynasty of the great gods.

### Cosmic Boundary

Heaven as the limit and container of the visible world, paired with earth below.

### Ancestor of Marduk

Through Anu and Ea, Anšar is the great-grandfather of Marduk, king of the gods.

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.

symbols.body:
His attributes express his identity as the primordial sky:[^1]

- **The celestial dome** — The bowl of heaven, the visible sky as the body of Anšar.
- **Circle or ring** — The šar element suggests totality, circumference, and the full circle of the sky.
- **Upper waters** — Heaven as the region above the waters, separated from the earth below.
- **Starry field** — The fixed stars and planets set in the dome of Anšar.

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.

mythology.body:
Anšar's mythology is concentrated in the Babylonian creation epic **Enūma Eliš**.[^1]

### Birth from the Waters

In the beginning there was only Apsû the sweet waters and Tiāmat the salt waters. Their mingling produced Lahmu and Lahamu, and these in turn produced Anšar and Kišar, the Whole Sky and the Whole Earth.[^2]

### Father of Anu

Anšar and Kišar together beget Anu, the great sky god. Anu in turn begets Ea, and Ea begets Marduk. Anšar therefore stands at the head of the divine genealogy.[^3]

### The Council of the Gods

When Tiāmat raises an army of monsters, Anšar summons the divine council and appoints Marduk as champion to face her. His authority is that of the senior ancestor, the voice of cosmic order against chaos.[^4]

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.
Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths.
Jacobsen, The Treasures of Darkness: A History of Mesopotamian Religion.

syncretism.body:
Anšar has no extensive independent cult or foreign syncretisms. His importance is entirely cosmogonic: he is the primordial sky from whom the later sky god Anu descends.[^1] The Greek Ouranos and the Egyptian Nut share the role of celestial parent, though no direct historical connection is attested. Anšar's primary significance remains his pairing with Kišar as the first cosmic differentiation.

Kindred figures in the PuniCodex cross-tradition index include [[kishar|Kišar]] (earth / primordial), [[ouranos|Ouranos]] (sky), and [[anu|Anû]] (sky / sovereignty).

sources.citation: Black & Green, Gods, Demons and Symbols of Ancient Mesopotamia.

cultural-legacy.body: Anšar's legacy is literary and cosmological rather than cultic. The Enūma Eliš, in which he appears, was recited at the Babylonian New Year festival and shaped Mesopotamian ideas of cosmic order for more than a millennium.[^1] The pairing of Anšar and Kišar as heaven and earth is one of the earliest expressions of binary cosmology found across Eurasia.

sources.citation: Foster, Before the Muses: An Anthology of Akkadian Literature.

archaeology.body: Anšar has no independent temples or cult images. His presence in the archaeological record is entirely textual, above all in copies of Enūma Eliš from Assyrian and Babylonian libraries such as Ashurbanipal's collection at Nineveh.[^1] The epic was copied and recited for more than a thousand years, ensuring the name's preservation.

sources.citation: Lambert, Babylonian Creation Myths.
